content: Adding zinc to the diet during infancy and early childhood has been shown to potentially enhance growth in children. However, the evidence remains inconsistent, with some studies showing benefits while others do not. In South Africa, biofortified maize enriched with provitamin A, as well as orange-fleshed sweet potatoes rich in provitamin A and iron, are available. These biofortified foods have been well-accepted and could potentially replace non-fortified versions in traditional diets. Micronutrient-fortified complementary foods may help prevent a decline in serum retinol levels over a six-month intervention period, which is critical for maintaining adequate vitamin A status. Micronutrient deficiencies are prevalent in lowand middle-income countries, particularly in South Asia and Africa, where staple foods often lack sufficient nutrients to meet daily requirements. Pregnant and lactating women, as well as children, are the most vulnerable groups. Consequently, many studies focus on the health benefits of dietary supplementation in these high-risk populations. Large-scale food fortification programs have demonstrated positive impacts on reducing goiter, neural tube defects, anemia, iodine deficiency (ID), and vitamin A deficiency (VAD) in children and women of reproductive age. Iron deficiency anemia (IDA) is a significant global health issue, particularly affecting children aged 6–24 months. In many developing countries, complementary foods lack adequate iron, making iron supplementation or fortification a potentially effective strategy to prevent IDA. Complementary foods containing substantial iron, such as meat or iron-fortified cereals, can help prevent iron deficiency during the first year of life in infants at risk of insufficient iron stores. Cochrane Reviews have evaluated the effects of micronutrient powders (MNPs) and lipid-based nutrient supplements in children. For example, fortifying foods with iron-containing MNPs at the point of use has been shown to reduce anemia and iron deficiency in preschool and school-aged children. Similarly, home fortification of foods with MNPs containing iron, zinc, and vitamin A has been effective in reducing anemia and iron deficiency in infants aged 6–23 months. Multiple micronutrient fortification has been associated with a 32% reduction in anemia, a 72% reduction in IDA, a 56% reduction in iron deficiency, and a 58% reduction in vitamin A deficiency compared to placebo. Lipid-based nutrient supplements combined with complementary feeding have been effective in improving growth in children from lowand middle-income countries, reducing the prevalence of moderate stunting by 7% and moderate wasting by 18%. Several trials have investigated the potential benefits and risks of complementary feeding with fortified foods. However, there is currently no up-to-date systematic review summarizing these findings. The objective of this review is to assess the effects of consuming fortified complementary foods (excluding milk) compared to their non-fortified counterparts on dietary and health outcomes in infants and young children aged 6–23 months. The review included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) with individual or cluster randomization. Studies with external or historical control groups, or matched cross-sectional control groups, were excluded. Participants included infants and young children aged 6–23 months at the start of the intervention. Infants under six months were excluded, as exclusive breastfeeding is recommended for this age group. The interventions studied involved the consumption of fortified complementary products, which could include a single micronutrient or a combination of vitamins and minerals. Examples of fortified products include corn-soy blends, wheat-soy blends, infant flours, pastas, breads, bakery products, baby foods, purees, sauces, snacks, and beverages. There were no restrictions on the dose, frequency, or duration of fortification, as long as the products were centrally processed. The comparator was the consumption of an unfortified version of the same complementary product. Studies comparing different fortified products without an unfortified control were excluded. Outcomes assessed included growth parameters (e.g., stunting, wasting), nutrient adequacy, nutrient excess, anemia, hemoglobin concentration, iron status, serum zinc and retinol levels, morbidity (e.g., diarrhea, respiratory infections), mental and motor development, and adverse effects. Long-term outcomes were also considered if participants were followed up over time. The review process involved systematic searches of databases, trial registries, and grey literature. Data extraction and risk of bias assessment were conducted independently by multiple reviewers. Risk of bias was evaluated using the Cochrane Risk of Bias Tool (RoB 2), considering domains such as randomization, deviations from intended interventions, missing outcome data, outcome measurement, and selection of reported results. For data analysis, results were presented as risk ratios (RRs) or odds ratios (ORs) for dichotomous outcomes and mean differences (MDs) or standardized mean differences (SMDs) for continuous outcomes. Random-effects models were used to account for heterogeneity across studies. Subgroup analyses were conducted based on age groups, types of nutrients added, types of fortified products, and duration of intervention. Heterogeneity was assessed using the I² statistic, and funnel plots were used to evaluate reporting biases. Sensitivity analyses were performed to explore the effects of clustering and other methodological factors. The findings of this review aim to provide evidence on the dietary and health impacts of fortified complementary foods in young children, addressing critical gaps in the current literature.
